reasoning.notes: Through rounds 1-12 the reasons are almost all the same line, "raise my own letter, it fits the plan." Reading rivals' goals was trivial because nobody raised a decoy. In the endgame the reasoning sharpens: players count No cards from the anonymous tallies, and seat 4 correctly worked out that all 8 cards were gone. Still, there are clear mistakes in the counting.

evidence.quote: The No votes so far add up to 3 + 3 + 2 = 8, and that is all 8 cards at the table.
evidence.shows: Correct inference from the anonymous No counts that nobody can veto, which won the game.

evidence.quote: Across the two earlier votes, seats 1, 3 and 4 spent five No cards out of six, so only one of them has a card left.
evidence.shows: Specific card-counting about the other seats' hidden resources.

evidence.quote: B is almost certainly seat 3's character, and seats 1 and 4 both have a strong reason to block it.
evidence.shows: Voting Yes to free-ride on rivals' vetoes and keep a card, as the designer intended.

evidence.quote: I hold the last No card: I voted Yes on D and B and No on E, and 7 of the 8 No cards are now spent.
evidence.shows: Tracked its own spending and the table's to see it alone could force the draw.

planning.notes: Most of the game is a mechanical even-pass ritual with no look-ahead. The last four rounds bring real multi-round plans: a pushing rotation, timing who raises first, and steering one's own letter to the final, unvetoable slot. Seat 4 in match 1 carried such a plan through to a win.

evidence.quote: If the others then level H and K, I raise first next round. That lets me choose which character gets pushed to 5, and I can pick one that isn't mine.
evidence.shows: Sets up control of the first forced push one round ahead.

evidence.quote: I'll keep that quiet and steer the rotation so my letter comes up last, where a full Yes vote would win it for me.
evidence.shows: Multi-round plan that relies on others exhausting their No cards.

evidence.quote: Nobody can vote No now, so the letter I push to 5 will be crowned. I'll keep the message neutral.
evidence.shows: Hides the coming defection in talk so the final raise can be carried out.

evidence.quote: Sticking to the agreed plan is the more reliable path to at least a shared result.
evidence.shows: Weighs the final push against what the last card-holder will do.

luck.notes: The deal is symmetric and was not decisive. Results turned on No-card exhaustion and on who is first raiser in round 16. That is fixed by seat order (seat 4 every time with 4 players and 16 rounds), not by chance, and it gives the last seat a structural edge the designer claims was removed.

evidence.quote: Final round, and I raise first. I have no No cards left
evidence.shows: The final push always falls to seat 4, a structural position rather than a random one.

weak_spots.what: Claimed "Seat 1 never cast No on J," but J drew 3 No votes while its owner seat 2 voted Yes, so seats 1, 3 and 4 all voted No. This misread fed the wrong card count used at turn 121.
Spent the last No on D, believing seat 2 had none, although seat 2 still had one. Holding it would have left a veto for round 16 and stopped seat 4's free crowning of E.

All three rivals vetoed J and later G (3 No votes each) when one suffices. This redundant spending exhausted the table and handed the last pusher a guaranteed king. Voting Yes when others clearly would veto, as seat 2 did in match 2, was the better-reasoned option.
"Hiding my goal gains little now" shows the pattern across all seats: no decoy raises at all, so every goal was public by round 4. Decoying, one of the designer's core skills, was never tried.
Pushed its own letter E to 5 under a "push your own" deal, guaranteeing its own loss first. Pushing a rival's letter also loses one letter for that seat and keeps seat 1's own letters safe.

summary: Winning came down to endgame No-card counting and timing who makes the final push, which does reward inference and a few rounds of planning. The first 12 rounds were a collusive leveling ritual with no decoys. More would be demanded by removing the fixed last-pusher advantage, for example by randomizing the round-16 raiser, and by making the goal-revealing raise pattern costly.
